Sadler's tetra (Brycinus sadleri) attains a maximum recorded total length of 13.8 centimeters [Li = 13.8 centimeters], a modest adult size typical of many small-bodied characiforms inhabiting the fluvial systems of East Africa. Field surveys conducted in the Lake Victoria basin have indicated that individuals of this species rarely exceed this asymptotic length, which appears to be a robust estimate of the ultimate size reached under natural conditions. Sexual maturation in this species is associated with a pronounced shift in body size, with individuals reaching puberty at a considerably smaller total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters]. This marked difference between pubertal and ultimate size suggests a substantial period of post-maturation growth, a life-history strategy commonly observed in iteroparous tropical fishes that face variable food availability and predation regimes across their ontogeny. Females at the onset of reproductive maturity exhibit a correspondingly moderate wet weight, with a documented body mass at puberty of 2.6 grams [Wwp = 2.6 grams].

Reproductive output in Brycinus sadleri has been the subject of detailed investigation under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. At this temperature, gravid females can produce a remarkably high fecundity of approximately 7,300 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 7,300 eggs per spawning event], a number derived from scaling the fecundity of the larger congener Alestes baremoze by body mass. The species is capable of producing approximately 1 spawning event per 18 days [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per 18 days], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate that is estimated at approximately 20 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 20 eggs per day] under these controlled thermal conditions. This reproductive strategy, combining a moderately large clutch with a compressed spawning interval, is interpreted as an adaptation to ephemeral and resource-pulsed aquatic habitats.

Embryonic development in Sadler's tetra proceeds rapidly at the species' preferred thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Under these conditions, the incubation period from egg fertilisation to the emergence of a yolk-sac larva is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This brief embryonic phase is characteristic of many tropical pelagic-spawning cypriniforms that develop in warm, oxygen-rich waters. The newly emerged larvae are initially endotrophic, relying entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves to sustain early development before the onset of exogenous feeding. At the moment of eclosion, each prolarva carries a minute wet weight of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the size of the fertilised egg. This extremely low neonatal mass represents a high-risk life-history stage, a pattern common among small-bodied characids that produce a multitude of tiny, pelagic offspring.

The complete lifespan of Brycinus sadleri has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance records, which consistently indicate that individuals can survive for up to 7 years [am = up to 7 years] when held at a constant water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This longevity is notably long for a fish of its modest adult dimensions and suggests a relatively slow pace of aging compared to other small-bodied characiforms. The ultimate adult wet weight attained by fully grown individuals reaches 31.5 grams [Wwi = 31.5 grams], a value that aligns closely with the predictions of length-weight relationships derived for the species. This asymptotic body mass, nearly twelve times the weight at puberty, underscores the substantial somatic investment that occurs during the adult phase, potentially supporting high fecundity and extended reproductive tenure.

Comparative life-history analysis places Brycinus sadleri at the fast-slow continuum in a position that reflects its tropical, seasonal environment. The substantial gap between its size at first reproduction (6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters] total length) and its maximum attainable size (13.8 centimeters [Li = 13.8 centimeters] total length) suggests that selection favors continued growth after maturity, a strategy thought to buffer against unpredictable spawning conditions. These life-history traits, including a generation time that aligns with the rapid early development duration of approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], allow the species to effectively exploit seasonally available floodplain habitats across its East African range at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C].
